column2: You should not take it to heart; it was not done by Drona's son; it was the grace of Mahadeva. Do the next thing that must be done.

Life, beauty, youth, accumulated wealth, health and the company of loved ones are impermanent; the wise man should not cling to them.
mahabharata:11:2.16	You ought not to grieve alone for a sorrow that belongs to the whole country; even if it were joined with non-existence, it would not cease for him.
mahabharata:11:2.17	Without grieving one should counter it, if one sees any effective means; this is the remedy for sorrow: not to dwell on it; for sorrow, when brooded on, does not go away and grows the more.
mahabharata:11:2.18	From contact with the unpleasant and from separation from the dear, men of little understanding are joined to mental sufferings.
mahabharata:11:2.19	Neither wealth, nor dharma, nor happiness comes from this grieving; it does not depart, and one falls away from the aim of one's work and from the three aims of life.
mahabharata:11:2.20	Obtaining one state of wealth after another, particular, men remain dissatisfied and bewildered; the wise find contentment.
mahabharata:11:2.21	By wisdom one should destroy mental sorrow, by medicine the bodily; this is the power of knowledge; let him not be equal to children.
mahabharata:11:2.22	A man's previously done deed lies down with him as he lies, stands as he stands, and runs after him as he runs.
mahabharata:11:2.23	In whatever state one does good or evil, in that very state one enjoys the fruit of it.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "By contact with the unpleasant and abandonment of the dear, how are the wise here freed from mental sorrows?"
[Vidura said:] "From whatever mental sorrow or even happiness one is freed, from that the wise man, finding peace, attains a good state.
All this is impermanent, bull among men, when considered; the world is like a plantain stem, with no core in it.
The wise call bodies the houses of mortals; they are assigned by Time; only the true self is excellent.
As a man discards a worn or unworn garment and chooses another, so are the bodies of embodied beings.
Beings here obtain suffering or happiness, according to their own deeds, in this strange abode of Vichitravirya's (the world).
By action one obtains heaven, happiness and sorrow, Bharata; then one bears that burden, helplessly or willingly.
And as an earthen pot on the wheel is broken, whether when partly shaped or just finished,
By earlier deeds beings come to be and cease to be; in a world so established, why do you grieve?
As a creature moving in the water for sport, O king, may rise or sink,
so those of little understanding, rising and sinking in the thicket of the cycle of existence, bound by the enjoyment of their deeds, suffer.
But the wise, established in truth, seeking the end of the cycle, knowing the meeting of beings, go to the supreme state."
[Vidura said:] "From birth, hear all the activities of beings, lord: first, in the embryo, it dwells a little while.
Then, when the fifth month has passed, it develops by the month; then, complete in all limbs, the embryo is born in the month.
It dwells in the midst of impurity, smeared with flesh and blood; then, by the force of the wind, feet up and head down,
reaching the door of the womb, it suffers many pains, pressed by the womb and bound by its earlier deeds.
Freed from that, it sees other afflictions in the world; the planets approach it like dogs a piece of meat.
Then, in due time, diseases also approach him as he lives, bound by his own deeds.
Bound by the nooses of the senses, afflicted with the sweetness of attachment, many kinds of misfortune beset him, O king, and though assailed by them he is never satisfied.
He does not yet understand that the world of Yama has come, and, dragged by Yama's messengers, he goes to death in time.
Alas, the world is cheated and mastered by greed; mad with greed, anger and pride, it does not know itself.
Delighting in noble birth, it scorns those of low family; proud with pride of wealth, it scorns the poor.
He calls others fools and does not look at himself; he rebukes others' training and does not wish to teach himself.
In this impermanent world of the living, he who, guarding dharma, lives so from birth would attain the highest state.
Knowing all this, he who follows the truth gains the path to liberation, lord of men."
[Vidura said:] "On this I shall tell you, bowing to the Self-existent, how the great sages describe the thicket of the cycle of existence.
A Brahmana, living in the great cycle, it is said, came to a difficult forest, great, thronged with flesh-eaters.
Surrounded on every side by very dreadful great eaters of the form of lions, tigers and elephants, giving fear even to Death,
seeing it, his heart was greatly agitated, and his hair stood on end, and his body changed, scorcher of foes.
He wandered through that forest, running here and there, looking in all directions: "Where might there be refuge?"
Seeking a gap among them, he ran, tormented by fear, yet he does not get far away nor is he freed from them.
Then he saw the dreadful forest covered on all sides with nets, and embraced in both arms by a most dreadful woman.
The great forest was surrounded by serpents with five hoods, like towering mountains, and by great trees touching the sky.
Then there too another danger arose for him: at the edge of a well covered with creepers he saw a great elephant,
six-faced, black and variegated, moving on twelve feet, creeping gradually, covered with creepers and trees.
And on its branches, hanging from the tree's boughs, were bees of many forms, dreadful and terrifying, who had gathered honey earlier and sat in their hives.
Again and again they sought honeys, bull of the Bharatas, sweet to beings, with which even a fool is not satisfied.
From those honeys a stream constantly flowed in many ways; hanging there, that man ever drank the stream, and his thirst was not ended as he drank in his peril.
Ever unsatisfied, he desired it again and again; and no disgust with life arose in him, O king.
There too the hope of life was fixed in the man; black and white mice were gnawing that tree.
Beasts of prey at the forest's edge, the dreadful woman, the serpent beneath the well, and the elephant at the edge,
the fear of the tree falling, the mice as a fifth, and as a sixth the bees from greed for honey, they call this a great fear.
Thus he dwells there, flung into the ocean of existence, and does not come to disgust in the hope of life."
[Vidura said:] "Hear again; I shall tell you the details of this path, hearing which the wise are freed from the cycles of existence.
As a man, O king, travelling a long road, here and there rests from weariness or makes a halt,
so in the turn of the cycle, in dwellings in the womb, Bharata, the foolish make their home, while the wise are freed.
Therefore those learned in the scriptures call it a road; and what the wise call the thicket of existence is the forest.
This is the whirl of the world for mortals, bull of the Bharatas; the wise man should not cling to it, to moving or unmoving things.
The diseases of mortals, bodily and mental, visible and invisible, are called beasts of prey by the wise.
Tormented ever by these and struck down, Bharata, those of little wit by their own deeds are not alarmed by the great beasts.
Even if a man is freed from those diseases, old age afterwards, destroyer of beauty, covers him.
Sinking in the great mire on every side without support, among sounds, forms, tastes, touches and various odours,
years, seasons, months, fortnights, days, nights and twilights gradually despoil his beauty and his life.
These are the treasures of Time; the foolish do not know them; here, they say, all beings are inscribed by their deeds.
They call the body the chariot of beings, the self the charioteer, the senses the horses, and action and intellect the reins.
One who runs after the speed of those running horses revolves like a wheel in this wheel of the cycle of existence.
One who controls them by intellect is the driver, and does not return; they call this chariot Yama's, by which the foolish are bewildered.
He attains what you have attained, O king: the loss of kingdom, friends and sons, Bharata.
This sorrow is a thing of craving, Bharata; the good man should practise the remedy for the greatest sorrows.
Neither valour, nor wealth, nor friend, nor companion frees one from sorrow as the self steady in restraint does.
Therefore, resorting to friendliness and acquiring good conduct, Bharata, self-control, renunciation and carefulness are the three horses of Brahma.
One who stands on the chariot of the mind joined to the reins of good conduct, casting off the fear of death, O king, goes to the world of Brahma."
Sanjaya, friends and others, and the doorkeepers who were trusted by him, with cool, pleasant water and palm-leaf fans, Bharata,
touching his body with their hands and fanning him diligently, attended Dhritarashtra for a long time in that state.
After a long time, the king regained consciousness and lamented long, flooded with grief for his sons.

Fie on human life, and on human attachment, from which sorrows arise again and again.
mahabharata:11:8.7	In the loss of sons and wealth, and of kinsmen and relatives, one meets with very great grief, like poison and fire, lord,
mahabharata:11:8.8	by which the limbs burn, by which wisdom perishes, overcome by which a man thinks highly of death.
mahabharata:11:8.9	This calamity has come to me through the reversal of fortune, and I shall do that very thing today, best of the twice-born.
[Vyasa said:] "This son of yours, O king, was born for the destruction of the world as a part of Kali in the womb of Gandhari, lord.
Intolerant, fickle, angry and hard to rule, and his brothers likewise by fate were born;
his uncle Shakuni and Karna as his chief friend, kings gathered together on earth for its destruction. Mighty-armed one, Narada knows this truly.
Your sons perished through their own fault, lord of the earth; do not grieve for them, king of kings, for there is no reason for grief.
The Pandavas did not wrong you in the least, Bharata; it was your wicked sons by whom this earth was destroyed.
And by Narada, good fortune to you, it was announced beforehand without doubt in Yudhishthira's assembly at the Rajasuya:
'The Pandavas and Kauravas, meeting each other, will not remain, son of Kunti; do what is your duty.'
Hearing Narada's word, the Pandavas then grieved; all this eternal secret of the gods has been told to you.
How can your grief end, lord, and compassion for life and affection for the Pandavas arise, knowing the ordinance made by fate?
And this matter, mighty-armed one, was heard by me earlier and told to the king of dharma at his excellent Rajasuya sacrifice.
Effort was made by the son of Dharma when I told him the secret, to avoid strife among the Kauravas, but fate is stronger.
The ordinance cannot be transgressed in any way, O king, by any being, moving or unmoving, nor by force of the Ender.
You, devoted to action and best in wisdom, Bharata, are bewildered, though knowing the coming and going of beings.
Seeing you burning with grief and bewildered again and again, King Yudhishthira would even give up his life.
He is ever compassionate, heroic, even toward creatures born as animals; how then would he not show compassion to you, king of kings?
By my command, because the ordinance cannot be turned back, and out of compassion for the Pandavas, preserve your life, Bharata.
If you conduct yourself so, fame will be yours in the world, and very great dharma, dear one, and austerity long practised.
The fire kindled by grief for sons, great king, extinguish always with the water of wisdom."
Hearing these words of Vyasa of immeasurable splendour, Dhritarashtra reflected a moment and said:

I am driven by a great net of sorrow, best of the twice-born; I do not know myself, being bewildered again and again.
mahabharata:11:8.47	But hearing this word of yours, born of the ordinance of fate, I shall preserve my life and shall try not to grieve.
Hearing these words, Vyasa, son of Satyavati, vanished right there, O king of kings, from before Dhritarashtra.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing this, best of men, he reflected long, lost in thought, and said to Vidura, "Yoke Sanjaya (my chariot)."
Quickly bring Gandhari and all the Bharata women, taking Kunti, the daughter-in-law, and the other women who are there.
Having said this to Vidura, best of those who know dharma, the righteous one, his knowledge overcome by grief, took to his vehicle.
And Gandhari, afflicted with grief, urged by her husband's word, with Kunti and the women, went to where the king was.
Reaching the king, greatly sunk in grief, they greeted one another and cried out loudly.
Kshatta (Vidura), more afflicted than they, comforted them, and placing the tearful women in the vehicles he left the city.
Then a wail arose in all the Kuru houses, and the whole city, down to the children, was wasted with grief.
The women who had never been seen before even by hosts of gods were now seen by ordinary people, their lords slain.
Those rising bands of women, afflicted with grief, ran by many hundreds, O king, like young girls in a courtyard.
Raising their arms and crying out for sons, brothers and fathers, they seemed to show the destruction of the world at the end of the age.
Lamenting, weeping, running here and there, their wits struck by grief, they did not know what was to be done.
Women who had once been shy before their own friends were now in a single garment, shameless, before their mothers-in-law.
Those who used to console one another in the smallest griefs, distraught with sorrow, ignored one another, O king.
Surrounded by thousands of those weeping women, the king, wretched, quickly left the city for the battlefield.
Artisans, merchants, Vaishyas and all those who lived by any work put the king in front and went out of the city.
From those crying out, in distress at the destruction of the Kurus, a great noise arose, shaking the worlds.
As at the arrival of the end of the age, beings thought, "The end of all beings has come," as though burning.
Greatly agitated in mind, those townspeople, devoted to the Kurus, cried out loudly at the destruction of the Kurus, great king.
Seeing the king, whose eye was wisdom, the lord, they, their throats choked with tears, sighing, said this to him as he wept:

Your son, great king, having done a very hard deed, has gone to the world of Shakra, the lord of the earth, with his followers.
mahabharata:11:10.4	We three chariot-warriors alone are freed from Duryodhana's host; all else of your army, bull of the Bharatas, is destroyed.
Having said this to the king, Kripa Sharadvata then said to Gandhari, afflicted with grief for her sons:

Fearless in fighting, slaying many hosts of foes and doing heroic deeds, your sons have met their death.
mahabharata:11:10.7	Surely, having attained stainless worlds won by weapons, they sport, taking shining bodies, like immortals.
mahabharata:11:10.8	No hero fighting ever turned his face away, nor was any slain by a weapon with joined palms.
mahabharata:11:10.9	This they call the ancient supreme state of a kshatriya: death by the weapon in battle; you ought not to grieve for them.
mahabharata:11:10.10	Nor do their enemies, the Pandavas, prosper, queen; hear what was done by us, led by Ashvatthaman.
mahabharata:11:10.11	Hearing that your son was slain unrighteously by Bhimasena, we entered the sleeping camp and made slaughter of the Pandavas.
mahabharata:11:10.12	The Panchalas are all slain, led by Dhrishtadyumna, and the sons of Drupada and the sons of Draupadi are felled.
mahabharata:11:10.13	Having thus slaughtered the host of the enemies of your sons, we fled; we three cannot stand in battle.
mahabharata:11:10.14	Those heroic great archers, the Pandavas, will come quickly, fallen under the sway of anger and wishing to repay the enmity.
mahabharata:11:10.15	Hearing that their sons were slain while careless, those bulls among men, heroes, will quickly follow our track, renowned lady.
mahabharata:11:10.16	Having wronged the Pandavas, we dare not remain; give us leave, queen, and do not set your mind on grief.
mahabharata:11:10.17	King, give us leave, take up the highest fortitude, and look to the end and to the kshatriya dharma alone.
Having said this to the king and circumambulated him, Kripa, Kritavarman and Drona's son, Bharata,
looking at the wise king Dhritarashtra, the great souls swiftly urged their horses along the Ganga.
Moving away, O king, all those great chariot-warriors, taking leave of each other, agitated, went off in three ways.
Kripa Sharadvata went to Hastinapura, Hardikya (Kritavarman) to his own kingdom, and Drona's son to Vyasa's hermitage.
Thus those heroes went, looking at each other, afraid, having done wrong to the great-souled sons of Pandu.
Having met the king, those heroes, subduers of foes, when the sun had risen, great king, parted as they wished.

Considering his friendship with Vasudeva in boyhood and Arjuna's friendship and the people's love, he burned inwardly.
mahabharata:12:2.8	In boyhood he made friendship with King Duryodhana, while constantly hated by you, by fate and by nature.
mahabharata:12:2.9	Seeing Dhananjaya excel in knowledge of archery, Karna went to Drona in private and said:
mahabharata:12:2.11	'Your affection for your sons and your pupils is surely equal; by your grace let not the wise call me one who has not mastered weapons.'
mahabharata:12:2.12	Told so by Karna, Drona, partial to Phalguna and knowing Karna's wickedness, said to him:
mahabharata:12:2.13	'A Brahmana who has kept his vows duly should know the Brahma weapon, or a kshatriya ascetic; no other should know it by any means.'
mahabharata:12:2.14	So told, he took leave of the best of the Angirases, honoured him and suddenly went to Rama on Mahendra mountain.
mahabharata:12:2.15	Approaching Rama and bowing his head, he went to him with respect, saying, 'I am a Bhargava Brahmana.'
mahabharata:12:2.16	Rama received him, asking about his lineage and so on, and said, 'Stay; welcome,' and was greatly pleased.
mahabharata:12:2.17	While Karna dwelt there on the best of mountains, Mahendra, there was an assembly of Gandharvas, Rakshasas, Yakshas and gods.
mahabharata:12:2.18	He duly learned weapons there from the best of the Bhrigus and became very dear to the gods, Gandharvas and Rakshasas.
mahabharata:12:2.19	Once, roaming alone near a hermitage by the sea, with sword and bow in hand, the charioteer's son wandered about.
mahabharata:12:2.20	Unknowing, by chance, Partha, he killed the milch cow of a certain expounder of Brahma who was engaged in the agnihotra.
mahabharata:12:2.21	Thinking it done in ignorance, Karna reported it to the Brahmana and, seeking to appease him, said these words:
mahabharata:12:2.22	'This cow of yours, revered one, was killed by me unintentionally; please forgive me,' again and again.
mahabharata:12:2.23	The Brahmana, enraged, said to him as if rebuking: 'Evil-doer, you deserve death; obtain the fruit, ill-minded one.
mahabharata:12:2.24	The one with whom you ever vie and for whose sake you strive unceasingly—while fighting him, sinful earth will swallow your wheel.
mahabharata:12:2.25	When the earth has seized your wheel, your enemy, valiantly, will strike off your head while you are senseless; go, vilest of men.
mahabharata:12:2.26	As this cow was killed by you, fool, while careless, so another will strike off your head when you are careless.'
mahabharata:12:2.27	Then he again appeased that best of the twice-born with cows, wealth and jewels, but he said to him again:
mahabharata:12:2.28	'What I have said would not be made false even if the whole world tried; go or stay, or do whatever you have to do.'
mahabharata:12:2.29	So told by the Brahmana, Karna, downcast in distress, afraid, went to Rama, remembering that very thing in his mind.
[Bhishma said:] "He duly taught him completely the Brahma weapon and its withdrawal, the ascetic to the great ascetic, undisturbed.
Having learned the weapon, Karna, delighting in the Bhrigu's hermitage, applied himself to archery with wondrous valour.
Then once, Rama, roaming near the hermitage with Karna, the wise one worn by fasting,
the son of Jamadagni, affection born of trust, slept, laying his head in Karna's lap, the teacher weary in mind.
Then a worm made of phlegm, feeding on flesh and blood, dreadful, of dreadful touch, came to Karna's side.
It reached his thigh and bit, drinking blood, and from fear of his teacher he could neither throw it off nor kill it.
Bitten thus by that worm, Bharata, fearing to wake his teacher, the charioteer's son endured it."
The Sun, Moon, Vishnu, the waters, Wind, Shatakratu, Fire, Sky, Earth, Mitra, the herbs and the Vasus,
Having done this great slaughter of kinsmen, best of the twice-born, I cannot give even a small gift, and I have no wealth.
The Kaurava (Bhima) followed the wise Yudhishthira, son of Dharma, who was following the king, with his heart turned away.
Ornaments, parasols, banners and armour were seen being carried off by terrifying Rakshasas.
Then the wise Sahadeva fell to the ground, and seeing him fallen too, Bhima said to the king:
Noticing that stench, he said to the divine messenger, "How far must we go along a road such as this?"
